utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. A few and very short procedural matters. First one, the first has filed its 16th application for issuance of a subpoena ad testificandum which was filed the 21st of June, in which a date is mentioned of the 3rd of July. Mr. Re, as far as the Chamber is aware, that's far too short. Could you please provide, not necessarily immediately, but a new date because if we issue a subpoena then of course to start with the date should be correct. Just for you to consider. Then I'd like to turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I agreed, Mr. Emmerson, but perhaps not in very clear words in your suggestion, your very practical suggestion, how to deal with exhibits, the exhibits yesterday used in the context of the testimony of Bogdan Tomas. The Chamber has given it some additional thought, and for a fair procedure it should be clear for the Prosecution after every witness or after the cross-examination of a witness, whether any of the documents, even if portions are read, whether you want to tender these documents. Because if at a later stage you would tender the documents, a couple of pages, perhaps the whole of the document itself, whether short or a long document, the Prosecution should be aware what you are seeking to be admitted into evidence. For that reason, not necessarily at this very moment, but could you please prepare that maybe even later this afternoon, that the Chamber will be informed about which documents in the yellow bundle that are not yet in evidence you would seek to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to the witness Tomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Some of the documents in that bundle already are exhibits in the sense that they were exhibited in chief. For those that are not, I will make the distinction between those we are currently tendering and those that we're not tendering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- with you, I hope by -- before the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. And then, of course, with the witnesses still to come you might then of course in the context of their testimony decide that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Further documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- documents not yet tendered that you would like to tender them but then in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely so, since the bundle, for example, contains 92 ter statements of witnesses who are currently due to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and it is likely that they will become exhibits in some other form in any event. May I indicate, as I think I said yesterday, that yellow file is volume 1 of what will become a series of files of cross-examination material for the forensic witnesses associated with the Lake Radoniq part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour wants to move on to another topic at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I would like to hear from Prosecution and Defence whether there has been any agreement on the 92 ter statement of Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think Your Honour will see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand -- I just got a message that there is an agreement, so therefore the Chamber would like to hear what your agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- OTP -- well, I just read a note. "OTP has agreed with Defence proposal as to the redaction regarding Haverinen." If that's not true then, fine, then there's no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see a look of -- I see a look of some -- of confusion on Mr. Re's face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Astonishment. Astonishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just establish what there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me explain the background to that. Your Honour will have seen an e-mail from the Haradinaj Defence team making specific proposals in relation to highlighted passages in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Re and I lad a discussion over the lunch adjournment just before we sat in which my understanding of Mr. Re's position - he'll correct me if I'm wrong - is that pro tem, in other words, for the time being, the proposal put forward in the e-mail is acceptable to the Prosecution, subject to the Prosecution reserving the right to re-call Mr. Haverinen at later stage of the proceedings should they wish to have the passages that have been currently highlighted admitted and referred to and be the subject for cross-examination at later stage in the case. That's my understanding of Mr. Re's position, but If I'm wrong about that then he can correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is that your position or not? If you say yes or no, because if you say no, it's not our position, then there's no agreement and then the Chamber will give its ruling. If you say yes, there is an agreement, then there's no need to give a ruling -- at least most likely not. Let's not spend too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no agreement in -- precisely in those terms, no. The discussion at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- lunchtime in the cafeteria are not agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will give its ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that in mind, I think that the Balaj Defence has taken a slightly different view from the Haradinaj Defence with regard to this issue and we have submitted to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, it would be good that the e-mail submissions you made, that is, that the proposals --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- made to the Prosecution should be -- the text of them should be filed in any way so that it's on the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- What you suggested and there are slight differences there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because there are slight variations between them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- but above and beyond there, I think there's a different view. Our view is that his material should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does the Trial Chamber want the Prosecution's arguments precisely on the record? I know the Defense have e-mailed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you want, I can put them on the record what the Prosecution's arguments are. It depends on the ruling, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the arguments should not depend on the ruling, but I first finish -- Mr. Harvey, your position would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also sent an e-mail to the Chamber to indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have missed that, to be quite honest. Do you have a time for that? I'll immediately check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have it on me immediately, but it would have been at about 12.46, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that also explains why I missed it. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Essentially adopting the position taken by the Balaj team. I at that time had not had the opportunity to review the Haradinaj's response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then you join --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm joining with Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution's position is that the statement should be admitted. The material in the statement in which Mr. Haverinen describes what witnesses have said to him is, of course, hearsay. Hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal. Ultimately it's a matter of weight to be accorded to it. It may or may not be accepted; however, the appropriate time to make the determination of the weight or whether it corroborates or is the best available evidence is at the end of the proceedings. The Prosecution is not in a position at the moment to say whether the evidence which Mr. Haverinen gives of, say, for example, Witness 30 or what Witness 30 said is, in fact, the best available evidence of what Witness 30 would say if he were called to testify. That is something that should be, in our submission, revisited at a later point in the trial. If it comes to that, the Prosecution may, and reserves its position at the moment, may seek to recall Mr. Haverinen or another investigator who spoke to Witness 30 or any other witness who is unavailable and we cannot utilise Rule 92 quater to provide evidence of what a witness may have said, but that is -- that is the provisional view and we reserve our position in relation to whether we would, in fact, call it later in the trial. Our submission is it's premature to rule definitively on whether the evidence should go in. So in that respect, our submission, the evidence should go in and its ultimate weight be assessed at a later point when all the evidence is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I, for the record, simply respond but by putting three very short submissions on the record. The first is this. As I understand the position, if this material is admitted, the essential basis upon which it is admitted is that it is a statement made by someone whom the Prosecution would wish to call as a witness to an investigator. Now, plainly, if that were an appropriate and permissible course, it would follow that whenever a witness either chose not to testify or failed to attend for one reason or another, it would be open to the Prosecution in those circumstances to follow the same course. And I think that is the import of what Mr. Re is suggesting. In other words, when a witness, such as one we had recently, refuses to testify or when witnesses refuse to attend, the lacuna can be filled by calling an investigator to read to the Trial Chamber the witness's statement. Now, if that were right as a correct interpretation of the procedure of this Tribunal, it would render the Rules, and in particular the provisions of Rule 92, meaningless, because the Rules exist to govern the circumstances in which a statement of a witness can be read to the Tribunal where certain conditions are satisfied. Those conditions are not satisfied here and nobody is suggesting that they are. Secondly, the position so far as this witness is concerned is that he would not be being called at all were it not for the fact that Mr. Guy-Smith has been pursuing and is interested in pursuing cross-examination about the way in which photo-boards have been constructed and shown to witnesses for the purposes of identification. And to use that, namely, what is in effect the tendering of a witness to make him available so that a party representing the Defence can explore the manner in which identifications have been conducted, to use that as a pretext for in effect smuggling in hearsay evidence, in our submission, is not a proper course for the Prosecution to take. And thirdly, I am left in some uncertainty as to the position that Mr. Re is proposing because he suggests that the matter is premature for final decision, that it can be decided at some later stage with the witness being recalled if necessary, which is what I had understood his position to be, but that pro tem the material should be admitted. Now, as far as the Defence position is concerned, even though the admission of that material may be nil probative weight in the Trial Chamber's final analysis if those witnesses do not attend, it forms part of the record of these proceedings if it is admitted pursuant to the provisions of Rule 92 ter. And that is a record on which not only can this Trial Chamber rely but any other Chamber which may be called upon to review a decision can rely and on which the Prosecution can rely. And in our submission that is -- whatever the implications of a free evaluation of the evidence may be so far as the general Rules on a relaxed approach but nonetheless a rigorous approach to analysis of hearsay evidence, nonetheless to admit on to the record in these proceedings statements in this form which amount to putting an investigator in the witness box in the way I've indicated, to give evidence that cannot meet the requirements of Rule 92, is impermissible. So we would respectfully submit that if Mr. Re takes the position that he does, that this is a matter that should be decided later on with the witness being recalled, if necessary, to deal with it, then the interim position as I suggested should be that the highlighted passages are not admitted or are admitted conditionally on the terms that we had set out in our e-mail. That is to say that they're not tendered for the time being to show the truth of their contents. If the three witnesses who have yet to be called do testify, then they may be admitted and relied upon to show consistency or inconsistency but for that purpose alone. If they don't testify they shouldn't be relied upon or admitted at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, if the final next result of what is being proposed is that this material be admitted in the recognition that it has nil probative weight in the Trial Chamber's decision-making, then in our submission, it fails to cross the threshold of relevance which is necessary for evidence to be admitted, because evidence that is of nil probative value is not material which is relevant. To be relevant it must tend to assist the positions taken by one party or the other, and material which fails to have any probative value simply doesn't cross that threshold. Those are our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can line 22 be redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 22, yes, 22, 23, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I adopt the remarks made by my colleague Mr. Emmerson, and would add to them quite briefly which is that in the situation which we are presently in, those statements made by witnesses who have chosen to speak to investigators are not merely hearsay; they also are, in fact, at this time witness statements. And those witness statements above and beyond the concerns that have been raised with regard to Rule 92 also fall within the definition of and the concerns of the Milosevic ruling that I alluded to yesterday. And as such, it is impermissible -- and I will say it once again, it is impermissible for an investigator to testify about the summary of witness statements. As has been said, it's irrelevant before these witness testifies. Which is why I made -- I was trying to make -- I understand it was a belated suggestion yesterday but it was a practical one, and I said I think what we're really doing here is putting the cart before the horse, and based upon the submissions made by Mr. Re today it's very clear to me that not only are we putting the cart before the horse but we are potentially in a position where there are going to be two bites at the apple if Mr. Re does not get the evidence he is satisfied with at some point in time during these proceedings, and I suggest once again that the more prudent course and more practical course considering the number of legal issues that exist and abound with regard to this witness's particular testimony at this time would be to put him off to a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing to add to those submissions. I agree in full detail with everything that Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I be forgiven for one final observation on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very briefly indeed. I am simply concerned what occurs here has the appearance of being the thin end of the wedge, in other words as a matter of logical principle, if what Mr. Re is urging Your Honours to do is now accepted, then it is very difficult to see how on a future application, for example, if one of those witnesses failed to attend it would be difficult to distinguish between what is here proposed as a matter of logic and the calling of the investigator simply to read the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Re, is there any need to further --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe we're not really that far apart in some respects. I'm not objecting to provisional admission of the parts in relation to -- I think it was Witnesses 33 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a bit of a discussion of whether the glass is half empty or half full. Nevertheless, it makes a difference when you want to drink, whether you want to drink from the empty part or from the full part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber sees that you are not very far apart, and nevertheless, the Chamber wonders whether continuing the discussion for another ten minutes would bring you any closer. If you are only 2 inches away from each other, if you can bridge those 2 inches, the Chamber would have expected you to have done so already and the Chamber is fully aware of where the parties stand. If there is anything on the substance you would like to add, please do so, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Only this: If it's not clear from my submissions before, I don't object at this point to provisional admission, that's why I said before it can be a determined in finality at a later point in the trial. I don't object with Mr. Emmerson on proposal for provisional admission -- I don't agree with his terms for provisional acceptance of the evidence of the statement into evidence. But in relation to the point he made, and this is a very important substantive one, of the logical conclusion is that we could call investigators just to read on to the record what witnesses have said. Well, clearly, we don't intend to do that and wouldn't do that and we want the witnesses to testify. It would only be if the best available evidence at the end of the trial were hearsay, first-hand hearsay, we would then seek leave to possibly call an investigator to give evidence of what a witness has said. But that's a position we're reserving at the moment. And finally in relation to the Milosevic ruling which Mr. Guy-Smith referred to of the 30th of September, 2002, an Appeals Chamber decision on admissibility of Prosecution investigator's evidence, in our submission that's not applicable here. That was a situation where an investigator was asked to summarize the evidence of witnesses whose statements he had not taken. It was hearsay upon hearsay and was not the best available evidence. It was an attempt by the Prosecution to, in effect, put a dossier before the Trial Chamber which was rejected by the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber and hence is distinguishable from the circumstances here which we haven't yet come to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very briefly, if I may, I believe the principle remains the same. But more importantly for the moment I think we are beginning to slip down a very, very steep slope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. I think the Chamber is sufficiently informed to give a ruling, but give me just a moment to consider -- to speak with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Upon brief deliberation with my colleagues, all submissions made this afternoon are such that they were part of our deliberations earlier. I mean, we have not overlooked any of the matters you raised this afternoon. Therefore -- and also in view of the urgency of the matter, the Chamber will give its ruling. Unlike as usual, the Chamber has not written down for itself in full detail all the reasons, so therefore I give you very briefly the decision and give you some further explanation. The Chamber does not admit any of the highlighted portions in Mr. Haverinen's statement, and of course on the remainder we'll decide once Mr. Haverinen has given the attestation as required under Rule 92 ter. But the reasons I'll explain a bit further. So that's the decision. First of all, if I may take you to paragraph 2, page 2, of the statement where it reads: "Several witnesses informed us that ..." The Chamber does not admit that portion because it would be corroboration of other evidence. But since the Chamber is not able to see whether these several witnesses might be the same witnesses of -- as the witnesses from whom we heard testimony, the Chamber cannot admit this into evidence, which of course does not disallow the Prosecution to put further questions to Mr. Haverinen whether he could specify or what it was that he learned. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that point -- just on that particular passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to admit that one for the truth of that. It's just the background context to why they've compiled the photo-boards. That's not the -- that's not the truth. I'm not pushing the truth for that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in any way because I should have said that. When I'm talking only about the marked portions, it may be clear to the parties that what we are talking about is the substance of what the witness has stated and not whether the substance is true as to its content, that's what we are talking about. Then the Chamber has distinguished between categories. The first is the category of the witnesses that have not yet testified. To say it by numbers, Witness 30, Witness 3, and Witness 25. The Chamber excludes those portions because it expects these witnesses to come and to testify so that the evidence can be elicited orally -- directly from the witness and orally, and if there's any need to point at inconsistencies with previous statements, then of course an opportunity will be there. At the same time, the Chamber cannot exclude for the possibility that these witnesses will, for whatever reasons, not appear and will not testify. If that would be the case, then the Prosecution is -- can make an application to reconsider whether those portions of the statement of Mr. Haverinen should be admitted in addition to the portions that are admitted today. The portions admitted, mainly the portions on photo-boards and procedures followed in respect of those photo-boards. Of course, if such an application will be made, then we'll get a rather fundamental debate, I take it, between the parties, which will go somewhere between the Milosevic decision and perhaps the Milutinovic decision. The parties might want to raise at those instances matters as how to deal with previous inconsistent statements or even previous statements of witnesses who finally do not appear. It is well-known to the Chamber that not even in the common-law jurisdictions that views on that are always congruent. But of course the Chamber will then hear submissions in depth as what to do under those circumstances, and that of course would also include that the parties may insist on Mr. Haverinen then to be recalled and then not to be examined on the photo-boards, but rather on the substance of the statements. So to that extent, the exclusion at this moment could not be considered to be an exclusion forever. Another category would be the witnesses who have testified. Witness 6, Witness 21, and one witness who testified under his own name, Ded Krasniqi. The Chamber does not admit the statement of Mr. Haverinen in respect of the statements given by these witnesses, since ample opportunity has been there to elicit from those witnesses whatever the parties consider to be relevant and to put to the witnesses whether the previous statements were consistent or not consistent. So that's for this category the reason why the Chamber does not admit the redacted portions in relation to Witness 6, Witness 21, and Witness Ded Krasniqi. Then there is another, I would say, very small category. That's Witness 8, which has specifically been addressed in the submissions by the parties. The Chamber has not admitted the redacted portions of Mr. Haverinen's statements in relation to Witness 8 for the same reasons as the Chamber has given in its decision not to call the witness, not to call Witness 8 to complete his cross-examination. As said in that decision, if any new evidence that the Chamber would hear would shed new light on reliability, credibility, of that witness, that of course might have consequences as well for the exclusion of those portions of Mr. Haverinen's statement dealing with the substance of the statements given by Witness 8. Mr. Re, you are invited to prepare a redacted statement for admission, not immediately, but I think it's -- of course we would need to have a redacted statement if we want to admit a 92 ter statement. This is the ruling of the Chamber on the matter. Yes. The Chamber would very much like to proceed as quickly as possible now to the examination of Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I detain Your Honours just for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In relation to the planning of the next two days' hearings. The -- the next-but-one witness; in other words, not the witness to follow Mr. Haverinen but the one who is due to come after that in respect of whom there's an outstanding protective measures application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Covers quite a morass of detail concerning the investigations around Lake Radoniq, and towards the back end of last week we received a file of exhibits to his witness statement, not all of which were in translation, which contained some quite complicated data which has caused us to take some time on analysis. The translations continue to arrive, the most recent having arrived I think a few minutes before we sat today. I am in very serious difficulties being in a position either to cross-examine that witness tomorrow or to be able to comply with the Trial Chamber's ruling to disclose to the Prosecution the material I will wish to use in cross-examination tomorrow. Having said that, I would have no objection to the witness being called in chief tomorrow, and it may be that that would be in any event as far as we will get, but I'm not going -- with the greatest of diffidence, I'm simply not going to be in a position between now and then to have put the material together so as to be in a position effectively and economically to cross-examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's a related matter, if I may, very briefly. Amongst the material that that witness produces is a series of documents which purport to be ballistic findings and purport to support the statement in the Prosecution's opening that the casings found at the canal can be in one manner or another forensically connected to some casings that were recovered at Gllogjan on the 24th of March. Now, we have prepared a motion which we were planning to file today for the exclusion of that evidence for reasons that I don't need to trouble the Trial Chamber with at this point in time, but putting it very briefly, if I can, there is a missing crime scene investigation forensic report which is an essential link in the chain, but more fundamentally than that, there has been until now no reasoning or a detailed analysis of the forensic ballistic comparison, despite numerous requests from the Defence for more detailed information. And the casings themselves are not available for comparison by the Defence, a comparison we have been wishing to make for two years in the course of our investigations and with the assistance of a ballistics expert. At one minute to 2.00 this afternoon the Prosecution e-mailed to the Defence a statement from a Serbian ballistics expert, which I obviously haven't had an opportunity to read, but which may well render the motion that I intended to file -- may well require substantial revision of that motion in the light of what has been put forward. The short point is we are not in a position to investigated the ballistics. We've just been provided with a ballistics report which we're not in a position to analyse, and so far as I am aware standing here today, the basis for the findings has never been properly explained. Certainly hasn't been explained until the statement that was served at one minute to 2.00 this afternoon. Now, it is frankly intolerable for the Prosecution to be purporting at this stage to adduce ballistic evidence tomorrow and to be serving forensic statements on the defence when plainly it is a matter that they know we have been seeking to investigate for a very considerable period of time and have made numerous requests for the casings to be available for comparison, only to be told that they were destroyed in a NATO bombing raid in 1999 and that the material couldn't properly be examined. And so we're in the situation now where we cannot test whatever it is the Prosecution's wishes to put forward, but one way or another it makes the calling of that part of Mr. -- of the witness -- of the evidence of the witness to come as the witness after next and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- we're simply not in a position to deal with at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you could have referred the Chamber to the motion that you are about to file and to say that in view of the information you have recently received that the motion might need amendment and that it deals with your ability to cross-examine the witness and to make further investigations on this material. Because what you did -- well, it's not entirely for the first time, you put on the record not only your problems but also some blaming of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, and then we would now have to invite Mr. Re to respond to that and to say whether it was NATO bombing or something else, what kept them off, and the Chamber is -- appreciates that it is informed about future problems, but at the same time it should be presented in, may I say it, a rather neutral way at this moment and that at a later stage we'll hear from both parties what -- who's to be blamed for what. But if I would give now an opportunity to Mr. Re, that would further delay the start of the testimony of Mr. Haverinen, and we could have read this out of court at a certain moment as well. So therefore, Mr. Re, I'm not giving you at this moment an opportunity to respond, but I would like to -- to limit the -- the submissions to what is necessary for the Chamber for practical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should remind myself that I should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My only concern is that the Chamber should be aware that dealing with the witness after next in full tomorrow is going to be practically very difficult indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's abundantly clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by now, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am, just -- except for this. I'm just not entirely clear on which passages are excluded from the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The trouble is I couldn't print it out. When it -- the black which Mr. Balaj's counsel sent wouldn't print and it's slightly different to Mr. Emmerson's one. There's a few slight differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that for the time being let's focus on what the Chamber does admit, and that is all the evidence in relation to the photo-boards, et cetera, and that we're not talking about the substance of the statements of the witnesses Mr. Haverinen refers to. But if you need a break now and say in five minutes I get the copies ready, then we would have a very early first break, then we could proceed. I take it the parties are able within 20 minutes to produce a statement where all the portions highlighted by the Defence are taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have the one which Mr. Guy-Smith sent. That's easy. In printing it the black bits didn't come out, so I highlighted them myself. There was a slight difference I think in paragraph 20 where Mr. Guy-Smith wanted the whole paragraph out but Mr. Emmerson would allow: "I met Witness 30 on several occasions and I obtained signed statements from him ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 20 -- Mr. Guy-Smith is three lines. The first is that Mr. Haverinen met Witness 30 on several occasions. Is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is not a problem, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Signed -- obtained signed statements from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I do understand what is to be taken out is "about his abduction by the KLA and imprisonment in the KLA prison in the village of Jablanica during the summer of 1998." That's as far as paragraph 20 is concerned, Mr. Re. Any further problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 I think Mr. Guy-Smith wanted the words "having" and "careful" -- it says: "After having a careful look at the photo-boards." I don't think Your Honour referred to the words "having" and "careful" before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- at this juncture, I'm willing to concede those words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's no problem anymore, Mr. Re. Any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, Your Honour spoke about several witnesses informed us that Balaj was responsible for murders at the canal. This was one portion and the next portion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next sentence as well: "Because many witnesses named or spoke of Toger as a perpetrator and as the responsible person for the killings at the canal."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've got that bit. The next one I think underneath that which I don't think you referred to which was the last three lines from: "Who claimed to have witnessed Balaj's perpetration to see whether they could identify him from the photo-board ..." Your Honours didn't refer to that but in my submission it just goes to the reason why there was a photo-board compiled, whether they could identify someone who had done something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this paragraph, I think that the manner in which I've suggested it be constituted as sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then it's just the two sentences, Mr. Re. Any further problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm slightly unclear as to Your Honour's rulings in relation to the witnesses -- the ones who testified, as to whether it was the entirety going out or -- which the Defence weren't requesting or whether it was selected passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The selected passages in relation to the witness who had testified. As a matter of fact, all selected passages are not admitted. It's only for different reasons, for different categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if everything is now clear and if you could proceed without having the break at this very moment, which would be very early, then I invite you to call Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll do that. I call Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Haverinen into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out to you the text. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haverinen. Please be seated. Mr. Haverinen, you'll first be examined by Mr. Re, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haverinen.

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is your name detective -- sorry. Is your name Pekka Haverinen?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you born in August 1961?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you currently a detective sergeant in the National Bureau of Investigation in Finland?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have 20 years experience as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you spent 17 years in criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that include investigations of murder, bank robberies, organised crimes?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Any other things you investigated?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Well, it's a wide range of different crimes, but mainly the last ten years just international organised crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Between June 2002 and March 2005, did you work as an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before you joined the Office of the Prosecutor and you were working in Finland as an investigator, did you have experience with showing witnesses what are called photo identification boards?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are there -- over the years, how many witnesses do you think that you might have shown photo investigation boards to -- identification boards to?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Well, that's quite difficult to say the right number, but maybe ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are there guide-lines in Finland concerning the compilation of these photo identification boards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you would not mind, I had in mind perhaps to say at a later stage, but much attention was given at -- with previous witnesses to how they were educated in photo-boards, how long they took lessons in it, how often they did it, et cetera. The Chamber is mainly interested in how it was done here and whether that was in violation of what was learned or whether it was in accordance with the guide-lines, et cetera. That is of subsidiary relevance, and I would like all parties - it's now at an early stage that I raise the issue, but, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm reminding you of how much time that took in the examination of previous witnesses - it's of subsidiary relevance for -- it's not our primary concern. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just waiting for Ms. Schweiger to complete the redactions, which is why I was asking these questions, but we're there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Detective Haverinen, I would like to show you a statement you signed yesterday with a one-page correction to paragraph 30 that you signed today. And I've highlighted in yellow redactions, that is, parts of the statements which won't be admitted. Now, I want you to have a look at this. This is the unredacted version, so I don't want to display that one. Can I also show you the one-page correction to paragraph 34, which you signed today. Is that your statement signed on each page?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Both of them?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And does it represent the evidence you would give on each of the themes -- on everything in each of those paragraphs if I were to ask you questions concerning those matters there?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it's all true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that basis, may it be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, you have not fully covered 92 ter. The first is whether the written statement reflects what the witness said at the time; and then the second portion is whether he would say the same if asked today. I think you only dealt with the second one and not with first one because true and correct was not limited to whether it reflects what the witness stated when he signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With His Honour's direction, Mr. Haverinen, does that written statement reflect what you said at the time when you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the other matter has --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- been covered. Yes, please proceed. May I take it that you want to tender it? Madam Registrar, could we assign a number, although the redacted version may not be yet in the electronic system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P375, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the foregoing discussion, the Chamber considers that there are no objections and admits P375 in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And may -- there is also a redacted version, may that also be given the following exhibit number and we will do the redactions to the redactions during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that P375 will be reserved for the final version of the admitted document. Is that a possibility, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course it is, but there's a -- there are two versions. One's -- I'm sorry. I should have said. The redacted -- there are two versions we prepared: A redacted version and an unredacted one, one under seal and one not. So I ask that the first one be under seal and the second one be the public redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P376 will be the public version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Detective, I want to take you to paragraph 2 of your statement. A portion has been taken out of that. You will see it highlighted in yellow. I'm going to ask you the following questions. What was the purpose of your preparing the identification board containing the photograph of the accused Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: The purpose was when I came to the -- to the Tribunal, first of all, I -- my first task was to review the in-house material. And the team -- during that time the team was investigating -- investigating crimes allegedly committed by the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure whether or not the witness is reading from the statement or testifying independently. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't see what is in front of the witness and whether he reads anything or not. Mr. Haverinen, you may not have read at all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you're supposed to do. So it's -- you fully understood your task. For Defence -- to accommodate Defence counsel, sometimes witnesses will put at a distance whatever one might think people could read from, so in order to avoid any confusion. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: What were you told that led you to look for a photo-board -- or look for photographs of Idriz Balaj and who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: It was discussed in the team that we have to find a picture of Mr. Balaj because witnesses were pointing him out as a perpetrator. That was my task, to find a picture of Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Follow-up on that, pointing him out as a perpetrator. I want you to tell the Court, if you can remember, who the witnesses were or how many witnesses or whatever.

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: And I can tell here the witnesses' names. This is a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we -- depending on where this is going, we may need to go into private session. I also think the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there is a risk that the witness might mention names of persons who appeared before this court as protected witnesses. So therefore, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, without mentioning the names you just mentioned in private session, you said a moment ago that -- excuse me. You said something a moment ago about a perpetrator. I've lost it on the screen. I can't find it. Just excuse me for one moment. I'll find the passage. Okay. You said that witnesses were pointing him out as a perpetrator. Without mentioning the names of those who pointed out -- him out as a perpetrator --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that's a -- that's a misstatement of his testimony. He said he had discussions with his team. So there's -- it's one step removed hearsay already. He has not identified the sources of his team yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By that I mean the authors of his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He's just identified two people who pointed -- who said that he was a perpetrator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is denied. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Haverinen, the question was -- you said witnesses had pointed him out as a perpetrator. What did they say he had done?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at this point I'm going to object on the basis that we have had previous discussions about, it is not relevant at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, earlier you said you were not seeking to establish the truth of this. What then is the relevance? I take it -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think, as a matter of fact, it is relevant, Mr. Guy-Smith, to the extent of what type of crimes, whether we are talking about ordinary crimes, whether we are talking about crimes which fall within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. So therefore, you may proceed, and the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might briefly respond. At this point the state of the evidence is that he was working in the capacity as an investigator, investigating international war crimes, and that he had received information that there was a perpetrator by the name of Idriz Balaj. We need not go any further. That is the reason why he was tasked with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with the job of getting -- of putting together a photo-board. And that's the reason -- that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I do understand that you consider everyone always to stay within the limits of its competence because that's the implication of your observation at this moment. Mr. Re is supposed not to go in full detail, but is allowed to ask the witness what were the kind of crimes the witnesses pointed out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what type of crimes was he alleged to have committed as a perpetrator, leading you to go and compile these photo identification boards?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: At this time it has to do with the corpses, the bodies, that was found near the lake -- or the canal at least to Lake Radonjic. And the team had already interviewed a lot of people, and they pointed out that this spot where the bodies were found were actually used as -- or they said that it was Idriz Balaj's or his nickname, Toger's, execution site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- I object, and I think for reasons that the Court is well aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the same reasons as previous one, which was denied. Please proceed, Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are also now talking about geography, et cetera, and the questions put by Mr. Re are admissible. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that in the future we will not be revisiting this if these people do not come, because at this time it is unsourced multiple hearsay that this witness is testifying to, and based on this Chamber's view with regard to that issue, I feel confident that if that's the situation in which we remain, I have no difficulties; but if we remain in a different situation, then I have extreme difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Haverinen, I want to ask you about the OTP's guide-lines in relation to photo identification boards and procedures for showing these boards to witnesses. At the time, paragraph 3 of your statement, you referred to how you compiled the photo-boards. And paragraph 5 of your statement you said: "When showing photo-boards to witnesses, I followed the guide-lines of the ICTY. These guide-lines are very similar to those I had learned in Finland," and then you refer to the procedure you adopted. I want to take you to this part of those guide-lines. The guide-lines, which you say you were aware of, also contain a provision to annex a report when you complete a photo identification or attempt one with a witness. It would appear from the statements that you -- that you did not prepare any such report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We didn't use the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber why you didn't use a report and what you did instead of using the report?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: It was just decided that we'd put -- put it all in the statement and not to -- to make a separate report of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Actually, I don't know why, but it felt -- I mean, the outcome was the same anyway, so it was easier to put everything in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Who's going to cross-examine Mr. Haverinen first? Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Haverinen, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith, who is counsel for Mr. Balaj. We have another 15 minutes until the break, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what I said to Mr. Re is certainly addressed to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. There will be a few preparatory questions and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have been a police officer for some 20 years and during that period of time, as I understand your evidence, you have a fair amount of experience in investigating what I would call serious crimes and you have on, if I heard you correctly, at least ten occasions prior to working with the ICTY engaged in using photo-boards as part of your investigation technique; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: The number --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Give or take a few?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it -- it might be quite correct with ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of eye-witness identification and the use of photo-boards, before you came to work for the ICTY, you were aware as a police officer of the dangers that exist with misidentification, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a matter which has been discussed for some decades now throughout the world because of the number of miscarriages of justice that have occurred as a result of faulty identifications; correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if the witness is hesitant to answer the question, I'm not going to insist on him answering the question because you're asking him what discussion happened over the world in a few decades. You may be aware that the Chamber is fully aware of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge and your experience, you understood the dangers of this kind of evidence, and as a matter of fact because of your understanding before you came to the ICTY, understand the importance of following specific procedures in order to make sure that when eye-witness identification was used as part of the evidence against an accused it met all the requirements; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was something also of importance when you were working for the ICTY in your capacity as an investigator; true?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you first came to work for the ICTY as an investigator, were you given documents concerning identification guide-lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haverinen, before you answer that question, could I invite you to come closer to the microphone because there's some difficulties in hearing you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I told you already earlier, when I came to the Tribunal the first month I just reviewed the in-house material and what the team was doing. And I believe, because I know -- I don't know at what stage I read those guide-lines, but during that time, during the summer of 2002, I -- I saw the guide-lines and I read them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And were those guide-lines something that were discussed in 2002 with your team as something to consider in the event that you were going to be using photo-boards in your investigation process?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: It was not discussed more than that we knew that there were guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "we knew," who was on your team, sir?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: My team leader was Matti Raatikainen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Anyone --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Shall I name them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Howard Tucker, Roel Versonnen and -- wait a minute -- then later on during that summer or later on in autumn, well there were Ole Lehtinen and Jose Quiroz, Harjit Sandhu, Fernando Triana. There might be some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us that you were responsible for compiling a photo-board which included a photograph of Mr. Balaj; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in reviewing your 92 ter statement, you received, as I understand it, a photograph of Mr. Balaj from a source which is unclear, but it was as a result of him having applied as a member for the KPS or Kosovo Protection Service; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But do you know where that photograph came from, sir?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, we didn't know who this Mr. Balaj was, and I already know that the team had already obtained some photographs from his application forms. And from those application forms of the photographs I picked -- I found the application for one Idriz Balaj. I didn't know if that was the correct person we were looking for, but so I compiled a photo-board including with that Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The photograph that you -- that you obtained from these -- from these applications of Idriz Balaj, do you know what the date of that photograph was?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know as you sit here today when you obtained that photograph, the date that you obtained it? And by that I mean the year. Did you obtain that in 2002?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got the photograph in 2002 and you went about compiling the photo-board that you compiled, could you tell us the process that you used in compiling that photo-board?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Well, after finding a photograph of Idriz Balaj, I tried to find seven other photographs that looked like as close as Idriz Balaj. And think -- I can't remember for sure, but maybe it was a Power Point programme or whatever it was, I did it first on my own computer to pick out these eight persons. And after doing that I took it to the mapping unit and they finished it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that you compiled it in PowerPoint, I take it what you did is you made a determination that the individuals that you -- that you put into your photo-board spread looked as similar as they could to Mr. Balaj; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then after -- after you did that, after you were satisfied for yourself that that was the case, you then sent that photo-board, you said, to the mapping unit?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And where was that? By that I mean physically, was that in The Hague or is that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: No, that's in The Hague, in this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you sent your compilation to the mapping unit, I take it at some point in time you got something back, some sort of product you received back?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was that, was that a colour photo-board? A black and white photo-board?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: It was colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: And I recall that we received three different photo-boards with the same photographs of the same persons but in different order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You've just -- you put that in the plural, and when you did that did you receive more than one set of photo-boards for potential suspects or did you just receive the one photo-board that you put together with regard to Mr. Balaj?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: No. We received three different boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the subject matter, that being Mr. Balaj, did you receive any other photo-boards in 2002?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Later on in the team we compiled more of -- or other photo-boards, but I did only this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And all of the efforts with regard to the compilation of this photo-board in 2002 were done by you personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: I picked up -- I picked out the photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you picked them out, as you've told us, you received three sets back from the mapping unit which were the three sets which would then be used -- or the plan was would then be used to show the witnesses with regard to seeing whether or not they could or could not identify anybody in that photo-spread or photo-board; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: That's how I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the use of the word photograph, set of photograph, sets of photograph is unclear. I take it what your question was and that the witness understood it to be that you received a set of three photo-boards back from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before coming to testify in court today, you've had an opportunity to review the photo-boards, have you not?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've had specifically the opportunity to review the photo-boards that you prepared with regard to Idriz Balaj; true?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have I believe it's P364 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you -- after they come up, because they take a minute to come up. After you compiled these photo-boards, did you personally ever show these photo-boards to any --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- witnesses?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about that in a bit. I believe they're up. They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, is this photo-board, which is designated as U0157619, one of the photo-boards that you had compiled for purposes of use with regard to Mr. Balaj?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it - and just for purposes of our discussion - Mr. Balaj is in position number 6 on this board, is he not?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you had two other photo-boards also that were compiled at the same time by the mapping unit, and those would be seen in sequential order 76 -- it should be the next page. 7620, correct, Mr. Balaj --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Balaj is in position number 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the last one, if we could pull up the last one. And that's 7621.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Mr. Balaj's in position number 7; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate, Mr. Guy-Smith, on how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe half an hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson? No cross-examination. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I would think about 10 to 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Maybe 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until five minutes past -- ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see no witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we've got the time constraint, I'll just ask the questions anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not interested in the answers --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Guy-Smith, is that what you want to say? No, I take it, that the witness will be brought into the courtroom, but it gives me an opportunity to deliver a decision, that is a decision on a motion for videolink testimony for Witness 56. It's a decision on the Prosecution's motion of the 21st of June, 2007, for the testimony of Witness 56 to be heard via videolink. The Prosecution submits that Witness 56 is elderly and in poor physical health. According to a relative of the witness, travel to The Hague would be too onerous for this witness. The same relative as apparently informed the Prosecution that Witness 56 would be able to testify via videolink from the country in which he currently resides. The Chamber is somewhat concerned that the Prosecution has not been able to make direct contact with Witness 56 in relation to this motion, but has rather relied on the intermediary of a relative of the witness. However, we suppose that this has been due to the witness's ill health. In order to keep this decision in the public domain, I will leave out details tending to identify the witness. The details are found in the partly confidential Prosecution's motion. The Chamber has seen a medical assessment of Witness 56 dated the 28th of May, 2007. This was compiled by a medical practitioner, who based his assessment on two recent internist's entries for Witness 56 found in a hospital's out-patient log-book. The assessment specifies some relatively significant ailments suffered by Witness 56 as well as the therapy prescribed. While the medical assessment includes the statement that, and I quote: "It is our opinion that the above-mentioned ailments do not prevent the person in question from travelling by air," and that, I quote again: "I suggest that before any travel, the person in question undergo an internist examination for a second opinion," the Chamber finds that the question being answered here is too narrow. Instead, the relevant question is whether a person of Witness 56's advanced age and physical condition could undertake without great discomfort and risk a journey to The Hague, which is likely to last several days, and discharge his duty to testify. To us the answer is clearly no. Thus, the Chamber does not accept the Defence's oral submissions of the 26th of June, 2007, that a second medical opinion should be sought before the videolink motion may be decided. Given that we are not persuaded by the Defence's challenge and that we find the expected testimony to be sufficiently important and the mode of delivery of the testimony to be compatible with the accused's right to confront the witness, we find that the motion should be allowed. The Prosecution has tentatively scheduled Witness 56 to testify on Tuesday, the 17th of July, 2007. The Chamber invites the registry to make the necessary arrangements to facilitate the witness's testimony via videolink on or around that date. This concludes the Chamber's decision on Witness 56. May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You asked me before about a date for a witness I think from Serbia, the 3rd of July was the early date we had for a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The day before the one you just ruled on, the 16th of July, would be a very suitable date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then on the assumption that on or around 17th would not result in the 16th, the Chamber accepts your suggestion. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Haverinen, before the break we were discussing the compilation of the photo-board, and I'd like to continue some of that conversation with you with the following in mind. It's my understanding is you told us that you read the identification guide-lines, and there are a couple of guide-lines that exist in the ICTY, multiple photo-board identification guide-lines that I'm going to read to you, because I believe you were clearly familiar with them at the time that you were compiling the photo-board, and then I want to ask you some questions about what you did. "To ensure a fair exercise and to avoid influencing the witness" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- "the following procedures for a photo-board identification should be used: Use photographs of the same size and similar quality" -- and I pause here for a moment. I'm not reading all of the matters here because some of them I don't think really are germane to our discussion. "Use photographs of the same size and similar quality, nothing in the backgrounds to make any photographs stand out, and photographs of the same era, pick photographs of people of similar appearance to the suspect and similar ethnic background, similar clothing, and similar position. The photographs should show the same amount of the subject, all head and shoulders shots. Where necessary, police technicians can treat photographs to remove distinctive differences from backgrounds and clothing," et cetera. Now, I will pause there for a moment, and I take it that the things that I have just read to you are all matters that you not only considered but you dealt with in your compilation of the photo-board for Idriz Balaj; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: You can say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Can you say so, sir?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you had compiled the photo-board and sent it to mapping and received the three sets of the photo-board back, I take it what you did at that time was you reviewed them, the three sets of the photo-board of Idriz Balaj, to determine whether they were satisfactory for your purposes, which is to show the witnesses; correct?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I was satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think, as the witness is speaking the same language, please make a pause between answer and the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: For the interpreters' sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've just told us you were satisfied with the condition of the photo-boards. I'd like you to take a look, if it's up on the screen, of one of the three photo-boards that was in the set concerning Idriz Balaj and ask you whether you'd agree with me that with regard to the individual in position number 8, the background of that photograph is quite distinct from the rest?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the background in positions number 2 and 4 are distinct from the backgrounds in the remaining positions of 1, 3, 5, 6, and 7?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah, there are small differences, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that the individual in position number 2 has on a bright-coloured shirt, whereas the remaining individuals in the photo-board do not?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are those differences which in your estimation could potentially influence anybody who was viewing this photo-board, such that they should have been corrected?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, it is a question which more likely should be put to an expert. I consider this witness not such a level of expertise that he could tell us whether a light-blue background could lead someone to -- to conclusions --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the background, when you got the photo-board back and you noticed, I take it - and I'm asking you did you notice - that the background, particularly with regard to the individual in position number 8 was different, I take it that you did not make any determinations to have that sent back to have it changed --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
