utterances.text: The terrorists who were in that area, the area of Djakovica municipality, undertook armed operations on all roads which were not safe at all. That is to say that neither the police nor citizens were able to use those roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, can we maybe avoid the word "terrorist," as this is a little foggy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify that at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: When you use the word "terrorist," Mr. Bajcetic, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: I mean an armed attack on members of police, kidnapping of civilians, and taking them in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And what information or intelligence did you have regarding the kidnapping of civilians?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: The first case of kidnapping involved a man with a last name of Tomic. He was from Djakovica. He was taken away and nobody knew his whereabouts. In that period of time, people simply went missing. The people whose bodies were found on Radonjic Lake had been reported as missing by their relatives, and there were also some Albanians who provided intelligence to us from the field. We received also information through operative work. So all of that information taken together was something that gave us an indication on where to start looking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how many persons -- what information did you have as to how many persons were kidnapped by the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've been waiting to see where this line of questioning was going because the witness has just given a very general answer and it is in our submission -- if that is the line -- testimony that Ms. Issa wishes to elicit incumbent upon her now to lay the foundation, the witness has referred to an individual called Tomic. We now need to know, if that is to be relied upon, what the information was in relation to that case, where it came from, and on what occasions it was said to have occurred so an evaluation can properly be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Emmerson -- Ms. Issa, perhaps you first respond to the objection by Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has generally stated that he received information from some Albanians who provided this information and that people had been reported missing as a basis of his information. I hadn't gotten to asking him about Tomic specifically, but this is more general as to the source of his information. And he also outlines the source of his information in quite some detail in the 92 ter statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you elicit this information as finding the reasons why the witness started investigations, not to establish that what was reported to the witness was necessarily the truth but just a reason to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then perhaps your next question -- you said: "And how many persons -- what information did you have as to how many persons were kidnapped by the KLA?" Whereas the witness had not said that the persons were kidnapped by the KLA. The witness only said that on the basis of the information, they had a clue as to in what direction to investigate, which seems to be more adequate description than you gave in your next question. Ms. Issa, the reason for investigation seems to be clarified. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say I understand Ms. Issa to have conceded that this information is not being elicited in order to show the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That being so, further questions from the witness in that direction are in our submission irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, for the purpose of that particular question, yes, Your Honour, but I don't believe that I'm conceding that for any further examination on some of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For all questions still to come, we'll see for what reason you put them to the witness, what the witness answers, and then if there's any problem with that, we'll find out. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Bajcetic, you mentioned that you had information about the KLA kidnapping civilians. Can you explain firstly where you got this information from?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: I've already mentioned the man called Sveto Tomic. He was employed in Djakovica. He went missing in early July. The information received was that somewhere along the road between Djakovica and Orahovac he was kidnapped by the KLA. The man was gone. His relatives immediately reported that, and we started an investigation to determine his whereabouts. All of these activities were aimed to establish whether he had been detained somewhere or killed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for one clarification. May I take it that the activities were aimed to establish whether this person had been detained somewhere or killed by whomever. I take it that you wanted to investigate that if he was detained or if he was killed, who was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a reason -- there were reasonable grounds to believe that he had been detained by the KLA. As for the exact identity of the people who kidnapped him, no, we didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you focussed your investigation on the possibility that KLA may have detained or killed that person. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You mention, sir, in your statement that the area of responsibility at the time when you were connected to the RDB in Djakovica -- or at least the part of the area that you were investigating was the Dukagjini Zone area, that's paragraph 14 of your statement. Can you explain what types of criminal activity you were investigating specifically in that area?

utterances.speaker: PEKKA HAVERINEN
utterances.text: In that area there were typical crimes committed, such as kidnapping of persons, illegal trafficking of weapons from Albania into the territory of Metohija, also digging of trenches and building of fortifications, arming of people. There were cases of shooting on police vehicles and shooting people passing through the area. So those roads were not safe even during day-time, let alone at night. People could not use them to travel between towns or villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Based on your investigation or intelligence, how many persons were kidnapped by the KLA in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, as I've understood it, this information is not being elicited in order to establish the truth of its contents, and so a question of that kind posed in that way in our submission transgresses that boundary; it's of that relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Unless we're now going to move into examining each and every one of the examples that the witness is being invited to estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, the problem is that we are talking about investigations on -- in relation to events, and in your question now for the second time you linked them to KLA, whereas I earlier tried -- by questioning the witness, I tried to achieve a better understanding of what an investigation means, that is, that you may have suspected people or suspected organisations, but it's very difficult to say who's responsible before you have investigated. In your question, again you are -- let me try to see whether I can put a question to the witness which might give you some of the information you would need and would not need similar objections. Could you please tell us what was approximately the size of the problem you were investigating in terms of people that went -- disappearing. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Logically speaking, even if one person goes missing and his fate is unknown, one must start an investigation. In this case, 30 or even 43 persons were mentioned. Therefore, we had to establish where these people were, who had kidnapped them, and whether they were alive at all. The second aspect is this: The roads from Djakovica to Pec via Decani were such that they were not safe even for police because the KLA was present there. They were armed, and I don't know whether I should refer to them as a formation, paramilitary formation. At any rate, they were an armed formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the number of 43. What made you mention a number of 43?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned it because at that point in time we were unable to establish the exact number. Various pieces of information remained. The most reliable information came from people whose close relatives had gone missing. However, very often it was impossible even for the relatives to come to the area where their parents or other relatives lived because they would have exposed themselves to a potential attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not exactly an answer to my question, but I'm looking at the clock. We have to finish for the day because we need another five minutes for another matter. Mr. Bajcetic, we'll continue tomorrow. We'd like to see you back at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, and I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, not about the testimony you've given today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Bajcetic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you asked for the last five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, as regards the next witness and the timetabling in that regard -- I see that Mr. Dutertre, who's taking that witness, has kindly come to be with us so that we can clarify the position. Essentially, as I indicated at the outset today, I'm not going to be in a position to cross-examine, although in practical terms it doesn't look as though we would reach cross-examination of that witness in any event tomorrow. He's currently listed for 45 minutes in chief. I understand from Mr. Kearney and ultimately from Mr. Dutertre, but I will see if I have got this right, that there is no objection to the Prosecution having to either commence or, indeed, conclude if we get that far, evidence in chief without the Defence having formally notified in compliance with the Trial Chamber's ruling the documents that are likely to be used for cross-examination of that witness. And so if we reach that point tomorrow, in other words, if we reach the point of the witness being called in chief tomorrow, then I for my part have no objection. I understand that Mr. Dutertre has no objection to commencing that witness's evidence in chief tomorrow without service of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, you can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We don't really need to -- we might waste time if we don't have information on -- we don't want to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that late disclosure caused this problem. I'm happy to see that both parties agree how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you very much. Secondly there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just wanted to say it was not a problem of late disclosure regarding this witness, my witness. This statement was given on June 12th, we had a consolidated statement today, but I believe that a priori the Defence was not complaining about this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It -- there are difficulties as regards this witness in relation to the service of the exhibits in translation rather than the witness statement, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not -- [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is happy with how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly the exclusion application as regards the ballistic evidence that that witness may or may not in due course be permitted to give --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please, could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And a little slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm trying not to hold everybody longer than is necessary. The exclusion application, I have agreed with Mr. Re, we would file tomorrow morning in light of the service that the report that we received this afternoon. It may be that Mr. Dutertre will agree - I haven't had a chance to discuss this with him - to postpone the calling of that part of the witness's evidence until that matter has been resolved. Then finally this: In response to a specific request from me just before we sat, Ms. Issa informed me that the Prosecution's current proposal for next week is to move directly to the testimony after the next witness of two forensic scientists -- the two central forensic scientists. I don't think there is any application for protective measures in respect of either of them. And I see Mr. Dutertre -- I can't see that there would be in practical terms, but the I'm waiting for the confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the protection measures, I could give you more information tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you an answer off the top of my head right now, so I reserve my answer for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding the first elements for the witness called tomorrow and the part of the statement that I may postpone, I believe that he's talking about the ballistics side of things. I would like to discuss this with Mr. Emmerson maybe outside the courtroom and we could solve this among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we would be able to find an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then finally this: Without mentioning the names, there are two central forensic scientists involved in the forensic aspect of the investigation. Your Honour will recall that on the 19th of March we filed an application with a list of the names of certain witnesses requesting seven clear working court days' notice of the calling of the particular witnesses concerned and of course those two were central to that. The Prosecution replied on the 23rd of March agreeing to that proposal, and on the 28th of March Your Honours incorporated that into an order. Now, I don't wish to be obstructive in any way, but as Your Honour knows, I am not going to be here next Thursday and in any event part of the proposal and part of the reasons for seeking that degree of notice is that cross-examination of those witnesses on what are potentially technical matters require proper advance notice and potentially, we were hoping to arrange to have our own experts in court to be able to hear the testimony and advise. Now, I'm going to look, if I may, with Mr. Dutertre to seek a solution that can accommodate all parties, but one solution may be for both of those two witnesses to give their evidence in chief next week, the one after the other, and for the cross-examination of each of them then to be postponed until we sit again. I'm not asking for a response or a ruling, but I am raising it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are now proposing a solution for what you consider to be a problem, and I think as a matter of fact in the ruling of the Chamber on sitting days and nonsitting days that we would try to make, to the extent you can use that expression, Thursday a light day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means not issues which were fully contested but rather other matters, as important but still not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we're storing up quite a lot of them as we go along at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is looking forward to hear not whether but how you resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Issa, perhaps if there would be a possibility to agree one way or the other with the Defence on where approximately the limits are, because I take it that the focus of the testimony of the present witness is not the reasons why he started to investigate but primarily what he found when he was investigating. And of course if you say that this is reports, he received that report without further substantiation, I think other sources of evidence would be more appropriate to be used to establish facts in that respect. And as I tried by my questions to the witness to explain, not everything is excluded there. To say was it a huge problem, was it a small problem as reported to you, but the concern of the Defence is that by briefly referring to reports the investigators at that time received that this might be, although -- might be misunderstood as establishing what had happened. That's the concern, but I take it that you'll find a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we can continue with the examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of Mr. Bajcetic without further interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.
